questions.q: What is the composition root of an application?
questions.explain: The composition root is where all "which class, which lifetime, which settings" decisions are made, once, at startup. Everything else receives its dependencies instead of creating them.
options: The base class every service extends
The one place, near the entry point, where the concrete objects are created and connected
The top-level folder of the project
The first module the runtime starts

questions.q: In a generated Task API, app.ts resolves TaskStore from the container for the modules, while createDependencies builds new TaskService(new TaskStore(), clock) for the routes. What is the result?
questions.explain: Both lines are valid TypeScript and the container never sees the new TaskStore(). Two places decided how a store is made, so there are two stores. One composition root prevents exactly this.
options: A compile error, because TaskStore is created twice
A DuplicateRegistrationError at startup
Two separate stores: tasks created over HTTP are invisible to the modules
Nothing unusual: the container notices and shares the store

questions.q: In a freshly generated ZudoJS project, which statement is true?
questions.explain: The names mislead: the file called container.ts holds a hand-written composition root (createDependencies), and the real container is created in app.ts and handed to createRuntime, empty.
options: src/container.ts creates the @zudojs/container container and registers the example resource in it
src/app.ts creates an empty @zudojs/container container for the runtime, while src/container.ts wires the example resource by hand with new
There is no dependency injection at all in a generated project
The runtime creates the container itself and registers every service it finds

questions.q: You add a PaymentGateway that is shared by an invoice service and a refund service, must be closed at shutdown, and must be replaced with a fake in tests. Where should it be built?
questions.explain: Shared, lifetime-managed, disposable and replaceable in tests: those are exactly the reasons to use the container. replace in tests and dispose at shutdown both come for free.
options: Inside each service's constructor, with new
In createDependencies, once per route file
In the container, as a singleton, registered in registerServices
In a module's onInitialize hook

questions.q: Should a newly created Task object (id, title, createdAt) be registered in the container?
questions.explain: A container wires services, repositories, clocks and pools: the long-lived parts. Data flowing through the app is created by those services while they run.
options: Yes, as a transient, so each resolve gives a new task
Yes, as a scoped registration, one per request
No: data objects are created by your code at run time; the container builds the app's machinery
Only when the task is saved to the database

questions.q: Why does the Task API create StoreModule and TasksModule with new in app.ts instead of registering them in the container?
questions.explain: Who owns an object's lifecycle should create it. The runtime starts and stops modules; the container creates and disposes services. The modules still get the store through constructor injection, from the one container.
options: Modules cannot receive constructor parameters
The runtime owns the modules' lifecycle (start, stop, destroy); the container only has to supply the store they receive
The container cannot hold classes that extend BaseModule
Registered modules would be started twice

questions.q: Which is not an advantage of constructor injection?
questions.explain: Fetching services later without listing them is the service locator pattern, which constructor injection exists to avoid.
options: The constructor lists every dependency, so readers and tests see them
The object is complete as soon as new returns
With readonly, dependencies cannot be swapped behind the object's back
It lets a class fetch any service it needs later, without listing it

questions.q: Why does this lesson register classes with registerFactory(TaskService, (store, clock) => new TaskService(store, clock), [TaskStore, CLOCK]) instead of registerClass(TaskService, TaskService, { inject: [TaskStore, CLOCK] })?
questions.explain: registerClass types the class as a constructor taking any[], so a swapped inject list compiles and fails at run time. The arrow function costs one line and lets the compiler check the wiring.
options: Factories are faster to resolve
registerClass cannot create singletons
The factory's parameters are typed from the inject list, so a wrong order is a compile error; the class inject list is not checked
Factories are disposed automatically and classes are not

questions.q: The Task API should print e-mails in development and send them over SMTP in production. Where does the if that chooses belong?
questions.explain: Choosing an implementation is a composition decision. A factory registration makes it once; TaskNotifier just asks for "a mailer".
options: In TaskNotifier.taskDone
In every class that sends e-mail
In one factory registration for MAILER that reads the mail settings
In a middleware that checks NODE_ENV on every request

questions.q: A TaskImporter must create a new ImportReport for every file it imports. What should it receive?
questions.explain: A single injected report would be shared by every import, the container would make it a service locator, and new inside the service hard-wires the clock. A factory function is narrow, typed and easy to fake.
options: One ImportReport in its constructor
The container, so it can resolve ImportReport each time
A typed factory function (source: string) => ImportReport
Nothing; it should call new ImportReport(source, new SystemClock())

questions.explain: The container resolved the factory function once, but every call of that function builds a new Receipt, with the id given at run time.
options: ord-1 ord-2 false
ord-1 ord-1 true
ord-2 ord-2 true
ord-1 ord-2 true

questions.q: Which class is a service locator?
questions.explain: A class that receives the container and pulls dependencies out of it hides what it needs. Its constructor says "I need everything".
options: class A { constructor(private readonly mailer: Mailer) {} }
class A { constructor(private readonly container: Container) {} send() { this.container.resolve(MAILER).send(…); } }
class A { constructor(private readonly newMail: () => Mail) {} }
container.registerFactory(A, (mailer) => new A(mailer), [MAILER])

questions.explain: replace rebuilds the singletons that listed the replaced token. Hidden resolved the rate inside its factory body, so the container never learned about that dependency and kept the old instance.

questions.q: In the Task API, which code may call container.resolve?
questions.explain: Resolving at the edges keeps every dependency visible to the container. Services, repositories and controllers receive what they need through constructors.
options: Any service that needs a collaborator it did not declare
Repositories, because they talk to the database
The composition root (app.ts, createDependencies), per-request edge code that uses a scope, and tests
Only the runtime

questions.q: Why can a service locator break the container's captive-dependency check?
questions.explain: A singleton that lists a scoped token gets a CaptiveDependencyError. The same singleton pulling the value from a scope inside its factory keeps one request's data forever, and nothing complains.
options: Because locators always create transient instances
The check only sees dependencies listed in inject; a singleton that resolves a scoped value in its body is never inspected
Because resolve ignores lifetimes
It cannot; the check inspects every call to resolve

questions.q: Why should tests call the same registerServices function as the app, then replace a few tokens, instead of registering their own objects from scratch?
questions.explain: A test that builds its own wiring tests a second composition root. Reusing the real one means the tests check the wiring the app actually runs, and only the outside world is faked.
options: It makes the tests run faster
A wiring mistake in the production registrations then fails the tests too
replace only works on registrations made by registerServices
Tests are not allowed to call register

questions.q: CLOCK is createToken<Clock>("Clock") and Clock has now(): Date. What happens with container.replace(CLOCK, { useValue: { today: () => "2026-09-24" } })?
questions.explain: replace is typed from the token, exactly like registerValue. A fake with the wrong shape is a compile error, so fakes stay honest.
options: It compiles, and fails when something calls now()
It does not compile: the value must match the token's type
It throws DuplicateRegistrationError
It adds a second clock next to the first

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: replace rebuilt the singleton for everyone who resolves afterwards. The reference taken before still points at the old instance with the 7.5% rate. In tests, replace first, then resolve.

questions.q: What does container.snapshot() save?
questions.explain: A snapshot holds registrations, not instances. Restoring evicts and disposes the cached singletons, so a store that was filled during the test comes back empty.
options: Every instance the container has built, so restoreSnapshot brings back their state
The registrations only; after restoreSnapshot, singletons are rebuilt from them
The registrations and the scoped instances of every live scope
A JSON copy of the container that can be written to disk

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The snapshot kept the registration, not the cart. restoreSnapshot evicted the cached singleton, so the next resolve built a new, empty cart.
options:
1
An error: the snapshot was taken before Cart was built

questions.q: Two test files share one container and use replace plus restoreSnapshot. The test runner runs files in parallel. What is the risk?
questions.explain: A shared container is shared state. Keep a shared container inside one file, or build a fresh container per test, which is the simplest isolation.
options: None: snapshots are per file
One test's replacement can be seen by another test that runs at the same time
restoreSnapshot throws when two tests call it
The container becomes frozen

questions.q: Why does the lesson add a verifyContainer step at startup?
questions.explain: Resolving every registration once, scoped ones inside a throwaway scope, moves wiring errors from "first unlucky request" to "the deploy does not start".
options: To make the first request faster
The container builds objects lazily, so a broken registration nobody resolves at startup would fail on the first request that needs it
Because the runtime refuses to start an unverified container
To freeze the registrations

questions.q: In an HTTP app, where should a per-request container scope be created and disposed?
questions.explain: The request is the natural scope, and the middleware sees its start and end. finally makes sure the scope is disposed even when the route throws.
options: In every service method that needs a scoped dependency
Once at startup, shared by all requests
In a middleware at the edge: create it before next(), dispose it in finally
In the repository, when it opens a transaction

questions.q: A service's constructor has grown to seven parameters. What is the best response?
questions.explain: Constructor injection makes the number of dependencies visible, which is its point. A long list is design feedback; hiding it behind a locator or an options bag only hides the problem.
options: Replace them with one container parameter
Use property injection for the less important ones
Treat it as a sign the class does several jobs, and split it
Pack them into an any options object

questions.q: Rewrite OrderNotifier so it receives its Mailer through its constructor instead of pulling it from the container, and register it with a factory whose inject list is [MAILER]. The program must print the e-mail line.
questions.explain: The constructor now states the one thing the class needs, and the factory's mailer parameter is typed from [MAILER]. A missing mailer now fails when OrderNotifier is resolved, not when an order ships.
questions.expected: to ada@example.com: Order ord-7 has shipped

questions.q: Register MAILER with a factory that reads the TRANSPORT token: "console" gives a ConsoleMailer, "sms" gives an SmsMailer. Then the loop must print one line per transport.
questions.explain: The choice lives in one factory registration at the composition root. Code that sends messages never checks the transport.
questions.expected:
console: Order ord-7 has shipped
sms: Order ord-7 has shipped

questions.q: Checkout must create a new Receipt for every payment. Register a RECEIPT_FACTORY token whose value is a function (orderId) => Receipt that gives each receipt the injected CLOCK, and register Checkout with it. Print both receipts.
questions.explain: The factory registration receives the clock once and returns a function that closes over it. Checkout can only make receipts; it never sees the container.
questions.expected:
ord-1 paid on 2026-09-24
ord-2 paid on 2026-09-24

questions.q: Write testContainer(rate): it must call the production registerShop, then replace VAT_RATE with rate. Two containers with different rates must not affect each other.
questions.explain: Each test gets its own container built by the real registerShop, with only the rate replaced. Nothing is shared, so the order of tests does not matter.

questions.q: Write verify(container): resolve every registration from container.getRegistrations() once and return the list of describeToken(token) names that fail. The broken container below must report ["Invoices"].
questions.explain: Resolving every registration once at startup finds the missing Payments before any request needs invoices. describeToken turns a class or a createToken token into a readable name.

questions.q: Complete handle(requestId): create a scope named after the request, resolve RequestLog twice from it, add one entry through each, and dispose the scope at the end even if something throws. Each request must print its own two entries when its log is disposed.
questions.explain: Within one scope both resolves return the same log, so both entries land together. Disposing in finally flushes each request's log exactly once, and a new scope starts empty.
questions.expected:
req-1 start | req-1 end
req-2 start | req-2 end

questions.q: A route handler calls scopeOf(ctx.request).resolve(TaskCommands), where a middleware put a per-request scope on the request. Is that a service locator?
questions.explain: The route is edge code, the per-request part of the composition root. The problem with a locator is a service hiding its dependencies; here the dependency graph below the route is still declared in inject lists.
options: Yes, every resolve outside app.ts is a locator
No, it is the one resolve per request at the edge; TaskCommands and everything below it still receive their dependencies through constructors
Yes, because routes must never touch the container
No, because scoped resolves are not checked by the container

questions.q: In the Task API, why is verifyContainer called in server.ts and not inside createApp?
questions.explain: It disposes its throwaway scope with await, so it runs where awaiting is possible: right after createApp, before runtime.start() and long before the port opens.
options: Because createApp has no access to the container
verifyContainer is async and createApp is synchronous; server.ts can use top-level await before the runtime starts
Because verification must run after server.start()
Because the runtime would verify the container a second time
